analysis.one_liner: Strips all federal funding from the Affordable Care Act and cancels its unspent money.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to seven House committees in February 2011, drew zero cosponsors, and never advanced again — it died in committee without ever reaching the House floor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would block any federal money from being spent to carry out the Affordable Care Act and cancel every unspent dollar already appropriated for it. Deauthorizing the entire law would have stopped the premium subsidies, the Medicaid expansion money, and the enforcement of consumer rules like the ban on denying coverage for pre-existing conditions. The bill got a single sponsor, no cosponsors, and never moved past its initial referrals to committees.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been people and interests who bore the Affordable Care Act's costs: higher-income households who would no longer pay the law's Medicare surtaxes and investment-income tax, employers who would no longer face the coverage mandate or its penalties, and health plans and providers freed from the law's rate-review, medical-loss-ratio, and coverage requirements. Ordinary people already relying on the law — young adults on a parent's plan, people with pre-existing conditions, subscribers whose plans could no longer impose lifetime dollar limits — would have lost those protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Higher-income households and employers opposed to the ACA

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that no funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out the Affordable Care Act or the health care provisions of the 2010 reconciliation act, and rescinds all unobligated balances appropriated for those purposes [S2][S3].

Ending the funding would have eliminated the outlays behind the law's coverage expansions, saving federal money and sparing higher-income taxpayers the ACA's dedicated taxes, since enforcement of the whole statute would be unfunded.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who had gained or stood to gain coverage and protections under the law: the uninsured who would have qualified for subsidies or Medicaid, young adults on family plans, people with pre-existing conditions, and anyone counting on the law's out-of-pocket limits and bans on lifetime caps. Funding the programs already in place would also be thrown into limbo.

drawbacks.text: Deauthorizing the entire law would have taken away protections that polls showed were broadly popular — including keeping young adults on a parent's plan, the ban on lifetime benefit caps, and guaranteed coverage for people with pre-existing conditions — not just the parts supporters of defunding objected to.

Rescinding every unobligated dollar would have left a fully enacted statute on the books with no money to run it, creating uncertainty for states, insurers, and hospitals that had begun preparing for the law's implementation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's one clear benefit was fiscal: it would have stopped ACA spending and repealed its taxes by refusing to fund the law. But the way it was written — a blanket defunding of the entire statute — would have swept away consumer protections along with the spending, and it would have left enacted law stranded without funds rather than repealing it outright. As written, the costs to people who had gained coverage or protections outweighed the savings for most households.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to seven House committees in mid-February 2011, picked up no cosponsors, and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Tim Scott of South Carolina introduced the bill on February 14, 2011, to deauthorize and rescind funding for the Affordable Care Act [S1][S3].

It was referred the same day to seven committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, and Appropriations — with no committee ever given primary jurisdiction [S5].

Within days it was also referred to three subcommittees (Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, Health, and Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions), and the action history shows no further movement after early March 2011 [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors and never received a vote in committee or on the House floor [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Affordable Care Act's funding stayed in place. The people better off are households who had or would gain coverage and protections under the law — young adults on family plans, people with pre-existing conditions, and future subsidy recipients — along with insurers and providers who had built plans around the law's implementation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Households covered by the ACA's rules

for.name: Tim Scott
for.role: House Republican from South Carolina; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip all funding from the Affordable Care Act and rescind its unspent appropriations.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split was ever recorded [S4][S5].

industries.note: Defunding would have cut off the premium subsidies that were set to flow through insurers and paid for a new customer base, but it also would have freed them from the law's medical-loss-ratio, rate-review, and coverage mandates. The bill's failure left the ACA's insurer-centered structure — subsidies routed through private plans alongside new federal rules — in place.

They stood to gain most from defunding, since the ACA's dedicated taxes fall largely on high earners and its mandate penalties on larger employers, while the lost coverage and protections would have fallen on ordinary households. The bill's death kept those costs in place.

Providers had begun preparing for the law's coverage expansion, which would have brought them paying patients while reducing uncompensated care; a blanket defunding would have preserved uncompensated-care burdens while upending implementation planning. The bill's failure preserved that expected expansion.
